# network-xray

> Browser view of why a router chose its path, read from the live state of FRR / Nokia SR Linux / Cisco IOS-XE (IOL) routers in a containerlab or netlab lab. It shows the BGP candidate routes and the reason the best path won (Best-Path Decision), OSPF adjacency state and OSPF-learned routes, interfaces and the routing table, as a topology view plus a per-router "DeepDive". Read-only: it runs show commands and changes nothing.

<!-- nx-llms-agents-20261107 / nx-llms-agents2-20261107 -->
## For AI agents (read this first)
1. A lab that is already running: do NOT run `./xray.sh <lab.clab.yml>` on it. It redeploys the lab (`containerlab deploy --reconfigure`), which wipes changes made by hand (it prints one warning and does not ask). Use `./xray.sh --attach <lab.clab.yml>` or the `docker run … --topo /lab/<lab>.clab.yml` line below.
2. Read-only by default: do not change router configuration. `scripts/demo-locpref-flip.sh` deploys its own lab, changes r1's running configuration and destroys the lab afterwards: run it only when the user asks for that demo.
3. `docker run -v /var/run/docker.sock:…` gives the container root-equivalent access to the host: confirm the user is on a lab machine first.
4. Keep the page on this machine: `-p 127.0.0.1:8600:8600`, `./xray.sh --bind 127.0.0.1`. `./xray.sh` listens on all addresses by default: say so. Open it to the network (`-p 8600:8600`, `--bind 0.0.0.0`) only when the user asks, and say that the page has no login.
5. Never print or send the contents of `network-xray.json` (it holds the lab's passwords) or the value of `NX_IOS_PASSWORD`. You may name the IOL image's default login (containerlab `cisco_iol`: admin / admin); never print a login the user set.
6. Do not invent values. Image digest: https://github.com/rclab-dev/network-xray/releases — from v1.1.10 on, the release notes start with a line `Image: ghcr.io/rclab-dev/network-xray@sha256:<digest>` (the sha256 shown for `frrouting/frr` in the README is the FRR image, not network-xray). If a value is not in these documents, ask the user or say it is not known.
7. Do not remove labs (`containerlab destroy`, `netlab down`) unless the user asks.
8. `./xray.sh` runs containerlab with `sudo`. If it asks for a password, stop and tell the user; do not try to get around it (`SUDO= ./xray.sh …` only when the user's account can run containerlab without sudo).

## Task → command
- Try an example lab: `./xray.sh examples/q21-bgp-lp/q21.clab.yml` (deploys it) → http://localhost:8080/ . Check first, starting nothing: `./xray.sh --check examples/q21-bgp-lp/q21.clab.yml`.
- Look at a containerlab lab that is already running: `./xray.sh --attach <lab.clab.yml>` (port 8080; no sudo, since it does not deploy; works with `--bind` / `--interval`; the collector writes `xray-states.js` in the repository folder as usual; stops with "is not running" if the lab is not up) or, in the lab folder, `docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v "$(pwd)":/lab:ro -p 127.0.0.1:8600:8600 ghcr.io/rclab-dev/network-xray:1 --topo /lab/<lab>.clab.yml` → http://localhost:8600/ .
- A netlab lab: the netlab tool (see Start); do not use `./xray.sh` on it (it would redeploy what netlab configured).
- A problem downloaded from Releases: its own `./run.sh` → port 50080.
- Windows: everything inside WSL2, in the Linux shell (https://github.com/rclab-dev/network-xray/blob/main/docs/windows-wsl2.md).
- Cisco IOL nodes: login from `NX_IOS_USER` / `NX_IOS_PASSWORD` (default admin / admin); with the image, pass them with `-e`. Only the global table is read (no VRFs). The image reads IOL with the plain `docker run` line too: on the default bridge network it reaches the lab's management network over SSH (checked with containerlab 0.82 and IOL 17.18.02). IOL takes about a minute to boot; until then the node shows "not ready yet".
- Open the page from another machine: `./xray.sh` already listens on all addresses; with the image use `-p 8600:8600`. The page has no login (rule 4).
- Show why a best path changes after one Local Preference change: `bash scripts/demo-locpref-flip.sh` (rule 2; it shows the answer of example q21).
- Read the state from a script or an AI assistant: `node scripts/xray-query.js state|why <path> …` or the MCP server (see Query). `xray-states.js` is JavaScript: `window.LIVE_STATES = { "<node>": {…}, … };` (one JSON object per node), sometimes followed by `window.LIVE_WATCH` / `window.XRAY_PROBLEM` / `window.XRAY_VALIDATE` lines. The per-node format is DATA-CONTRACT.md.
- MCP clients: Claude Code `claude mcp add network-xray -- node /path/to/network-xray/scripts/xray-mcp.js`; Claude Desktop and other clients use an `mcpServers` entry: `{"mcpServers": {"network-xray": {"command": "node", "args": ["/path/to/network-xray/scripts/xray-mcp.js"]}}}` (Claude Desktop: `claude_desktop_config.json`, Settings → Developer → Edit Config; other clients, e.g. Cursor, use their own file: check that client's documentation, do not guess the path). See docs/mcp.md. With `./xray.sh` the live state is `<repository>/xray-states.js`; with the image, save it with `curl -s http://localhost:8600/static/xray-states.js -o <dir>/xray-states.js` and give that file.
- Stop: Ctrl-C stops the page and the collector; the lab keeps running. Remove the lab only when asked (rule 7): `sudo containerlab destroy -t <lab.clab.yml> --cleanup`.

## How it works
```text
 lab (containerlab / netlab)          network-xray (on the lab host, or in the image)         browser
+-------------------------+          +--------------------------------------------+          +------------------------+
| FRR        docker exec, |<--read---| collector (clab-xray-collect.js)           |          | the page               |
|            vtysh show   |          |  every 1 s with xray.sh, 2 s in the image  |          | xray-graph-nextui.html |
| SR Linux   docker exec, |<--read---|  (Cisco IOL: every 10 s)                   |          |  (the default)         |
|            sr_cli info  |          |  writes xray-states.js                     |          |                        |
| Cisco IOL  SSH, show    |<--read---|     and xray-states.sig.js                 |          | every 1 s: GET         |
+-------------------------+          |                                            |   HTTP   |  xray-states.sig.js;   |
                                     | containerlab graph = static file server    |<---------|  if it changed: GET    |
                                     |  :8080 (xray.sh) / :8600 (image)           |    GET   |  xray-states.js        |
                                     +--------------------------------------------+          +------------------------+
   scripts/xray-query.js and the MCP server read the same state files from disk (no router, no network).
   Arrows point from the side that asks; the answer flows back.
```
- The collector never changes a router: it only reads (`show` on FRR and Cisco IOL, `info from state` on SR Linux; Cisco IOL
  every 10 s with both `./xray.sh` and the image). It writes `xray-states.js` and `xray-states.sig.js` next to the page.
- The page is static files served by `containerlab graph`; the browser asks for them with ordinary HTTP GET. There is no
  WebSocket and no push: the page reads the small `.sig.js` every second (the simpler `xray-graph.html`: every 3 s) and loads
  `xray-states.js` only when it changed.
- `./xray.sh` runs the collector and `containerlab graph` on the lab host; the image (`docker run`, the netlab tool) runs both
  inside one container, and `:8600` is the port it publishes on the lab host (`-p 127.0.0.1:8600:8600`). With the image the
  state files are inside the container: from the host, `curl http://localhost:8600/static/xray-states.js`. The image also
  reads each router's running configuration every 30 s to choose OSPF or BGP (`show running-config` / `sr_cli 'info from
  running …'`, read-only; Cisco IOL from the last collected state, no second login).
- Only starting a lab touches a router: `./xray.sh` and a release's `run.sh`, right after deploy, restart FRR in a router
  whose FRR did not come up (the configuration is not changed). Viewing the lab never does.

## What it is
- A descriptive renderer of live router state, not a simulator and not a config checker.
- Input: live state, read-only commands only. FRR: `docker exec <node> vtysh -c '<show command>'`. SR Linux: `docker exec <node> sr_cli 'info from state … | as json'`. Cisco IOL: SSH, `terminal length 0` and `terminal width 0` (for that session only), then plain-text `show ip ospf neighbor`, `show ip ospf interface [brief]`, `show ip interface brief`, `show ip route`, `show ip bgp summary`, `show ip bgp`, `show ip protocols`, `show bridge-domain` (login `NX_IOS_USER` / `NX_IOS_PASSWORD`, default admin / admin).
- Output: a web page (topology + per-router DeepDive) that updates every few seconds while the lab runs.

## Supported
- Routers read (by containerlab kind, see `VENDORS` in clab-xray-collect.js): FRRouting (FRR); Nokia SR Linux (`nokia_srlinux`, clab-srl-collect.js); Cisco IOS-XE IOL (`cisco_iol`, clab-iosxe-collect.js; OSPFv2 and BGP, global table only). Other nodes (Linux hosts, cEOS, …) are drawn in the topology but not read.
- Lab tools: containerlab; netlab (as a netlab tool, netlab 26.10).
- Protocols shown: BGP (sessions, BGP table, best path and why), OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 (neighbors, interfaces and their areas, OSPF-learned routes; the LSDB panel lists the routes learned through OSPF, from the routing table (`show ip route … json` / `show ipv6 route … json`) — `show ip ospf database` is not read; SR Linux is the exception: its LSDB panel is read from its OSPF link-state database), static routes. OSPFv3 and VRFs: FRR only. Interfaces, routes, OSPF, BGP sessions and the BGP table (best path) inside VRFs are read too; on a router with VRFs the Routing table and the BGP Table show one VRF at a time (a VRF button switches; the management VRF `mgmt` gets no button). The IPv6 BGP table is not read. A passive OSPF interface is shown as a state, not as a fault.
- Image: ghcr.io/rclab-dev/network-xray:1 (linux/amd64, linux/arm64). License: MIT.

## FRR fields it reads
- `show ip bgp vrf all json`: per path `bestpath` (true for the winner) and `selectionReason` (FRR's reason), plus `locPrf`, `weight`, `path` (AS path), `origin`, `metric`, next hop. The Best-Path Decision panel compares the candidates on these fields.
- `show ip bgp vrf all summary json`, `show ip ospf vrf all neighbor json`, `show ip ospf vrf all interface json`, `show ip route vrf all json`, `show interface json`, `show running-config`. An FRR that does not answer a `vrf all` command in JSON (e.g. FRR 8.4 for routes) is read with the plain command (default VRF only).
- OSPFv3, only on routers with `router ospf6`: `show ipv6 ospf6 vrf all neighbor json`, `show ipv6 ospf6 vrf all interface json`, `show ipv6 route vrf all json`.
- netlab `validate:` tests (bgp_neighbor, bgp_prefix) are judged like `netlab validate`: per-prefix `show bgp ipv4 unicast <prefix> json`, winner = `bestpath.overall`.

## Start
- No install (recorded demo): https://rclab-dev.github.io/network-xray/demo/index-bgp-lp.html
- GitHub Codespaces (real 3-router FRR lab, needs a GitHub login): https://codespaces.new/rclab-dev/network-xray?quickstart=1
- containerlab: `git clone https://github.com/rclab-dev/network-xray.git && cd network-xray && ./xray.sh examples/q21-bgp-lp/q21.clab.yml` (deploys the lab; needs containerlab and Node.js; usage `./xray.sh [--attach] [--check] [--bind <address>] [--interval <seconds>] [lab.clab.yml] [port] [template.html]`, port default 8080, listens on all addresses unless `--bind`) then open http://localhost:8080/ (from another machine: http://<host-ip>:8080/)
- Any running containerlab lab: `docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v "$(pwd)":/lab:ro -p 127.0.0.1:8600:8600 ghcr.io/rclab-dev/network-xray:1 --topo /lab/<lab>.clab.yml` then open http://localhost:8600/ (run it from the lab folder; `-p 8600:8600` opens it to other machines; options after `--topo`: `--port`, `--proto auto|ospf|bgp|static`, `--interval <s>`)
- netlab: add `defaults.sources.extra: [ <network-xray>/docker/netlab-defaults.yml ]` and `tools: { network_xray: }` to the topology, then `netlab up`; open http://<host>:8600/

## Query from scripts and AI assistants (read-only, no router contacted)
- Input `<path>`: a `state_<node>.json` or a directory of them (e.g. `test/fixtures/iosxe-q15`), the `xray-states.js` written by clab-xray-collect.js, or a directory of saved FRR `show … json` files (`frr-collect.js --from-dir` layout, e.g. `fixtures/frr-collect-sample/r1`).
- CLI: `node scripts/xray-query.js state <path>` (nodes, links, OSPF adjacencies, BGP sessions, counts) and `node scripts/xray-query.js why <path> <node> <prefix> [vrf]` (BGP best path and the stored reason; `reason` is null with a `note` when the data has none). Prints one JSON object (`--format table` for a plain-text table); errors print `{"error": "..."}` and exit 2.
- MCP server: `node scripts/xray-mcp.js` (stdio, JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line; MCP revisions 2024-11-05 to 2025-11-25). Tools: `lab_state {path}`, `why_best_path {path, node, prefix, vrf?}`, `list_routers {path}`, `ospf_neighbors {path, router?}`, `bgp_neighbors {path, router?}`, `route_lookup {path, router, destination, vrf?}` (longest match in the collected routing table; it does not compute routing) and `why_path {path, router, prefix, vrf?}` (selected BGP path, other candidates, deciding step), read from the same state as xray-query.js. It only reads the given path: no commands, no file writes, no network. Claude Code: `claude mcp add network-xray -- node /path/to/network-xray/scripts/xray-mcp.js`.

## Tests (Node 18+, no dependencies, no package.json; run from the repo root)
- `node --test` runs `test/*.test.js` (fixtures in `test/fixtures/`).
- Self-tests: `node bgp-parse.js`, `node clab-collect.js --self-test`, `node clab-srl-collect.js --self-test`, `node clab-iosxe-collect.js --self-test`, `node frr-collect.js --self-test`, `node scripts/hello-kf-selftest.js`.

## Limits and cautions
- The container is given the Docker socket (root-equivalent on the host): use it on lab machines only.
- The page has no login and listens on all interfaces: keep it on a trusted network.
- With netlab, `network-xray.json` in the lab folder holds the lab's values (passwords included) while the lab is up; `netlab down` removes it.
- Not for production monitoring. For checking configs before deployment, use Batfish. For collecting and querying state across many devices over time, use SuzieQ.
- Single maintainer; pull requests are not accepted (forks are welcome).
